order.topic: Making inferences and citing text evidence
order.requests: Quiz: Please write two short passages of your own from my notes (about 250-350 words each): one story and one nonfiction article. Both versions read the same two passages but get different questions. 8-10 multiple choice questions, mostly inference and 'which evidence best supports' questions, then one short constructed response at the end: What can you infer about the character? Use two pieces of evidence. Rubric: A 4-point rubric for the constructed response (claim, evidence, explanation), in kid-friendly words my students can use to self-check. General: My students are 7th graders, many reading a little below grade level, so keep sentences clear. Number the paragraphs in the passages so students can cite them.

notes: Header line: Name / Date / Period blanks, then a plain all-caps title with the version (e.g. THEME QUIZ - Version A).
One short directions line: Read ... carefully. Then answer the questions. Circle the letter of the best answer.
Questions numbered 1), 2) …; choices lettered A)–D) (her own sheets use (1) and a)–d); this is the closest the print layout allows).
Paired items labeled Part A / Part B; Part B always reads: Which detail BEST supports your answer to Part A? (BEST in capitals).
Evidence choices are short paraphrased or quoted details followed by the paragraph number in parentheses.
Prompts point students back to the text: Read paragraph 2 again.
Passage paragraphs are numbered [1], [2], ... so students can cite them.
Ends with SHORT RESPONSE (4 points) and the reminder: Remember C-E-E: Claim, Evidence, Explanation.
Self-check tip she uses: Ask yourself: If this were the ONLY sentence I had, would it prove my answer?
Plain, short sentences for readers a little below grade level; friendly, direct teacher voice.

documents.title: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ
documents.directions: Read both passages carefully. Then answer the questions. Circle the letter of the best answer. Ask yourself: If this were the ONLY sentence I had, would it prove my answer?

sections.heading: Passage 1: Ba-da-bum
sections.directions: [1] Marisol sat at the kitchen table in her black concert shirt. It was only seven o'clock, and the winter concert did not start until ten. She bent down and retied her left shoe. Then she retied her right shoe. Then she checked the left one again.

[2] "Eggs?" Dad asked, sliding a plate toward her. Marisol pushed the eggs around with her fork. She took one small bite of toast and set it back down. Her drumsticks were in her backpack, but she unzipped the front pocket three times to make sure they were still there.

[3] Across the table, her little brother Leo grabbed two spoons. He tapped them on the edge of the table: ba-da-bum, ba-da-bum. It was the same beat Marisol had practiced every night for a month. He looked up at her with a huge grin.
[4] "Leo, stop it!" Marisol snapped. "You're doing it wrong, and it's so loud." Leo's grin disappeared. He set the spoons down slowly and stared at his cereal.

[5] The kitchen got very quiet. Marisol looked at the clock. Then she looked at the photo on the fridge of Abuela waving from an airport. Abuela had landed last night. For two years she had heard about Marisol's drumming on the phone, but today she would finally hear it in person. Under the table, Marisol's fingers drummed on her knee.

[6] Dad poured his coffee and said nothing. Marisol did not say anything either for a long minute. Then she reached into her backpack and pulled out her practice sticks, the old ones with the chipped tips. She slid them across the table to Leo.

[7] "Hold them like this," she said quietly, moving his fingers. "Thumbs on the side. Now try it soft." Leo tapped very gently: ba-da-bum. "That's it," Marisol said. "You can sit in the front row and watch my hands."
[8] Leo hugged the sticks to his chest. Marisol finally picked up her toast and ate the whole piece.

prompt.A: Read paragraph 1 again. What do Marisol's actions suggest about how she feels?
prompt.B: Read paragraph 2 again. What do Marisol's actions suggest about how she feels?

A: She is worried that she is already late for the concert.
She is nervous that Dad will forget to drive her to the concert on time.
She is nervous about the concert and keeps fussing over small things.
She is worried that she will not be picked to play a part in the concert.
B: She is too sleepy to eat much this early in the day.
She is too nervous about the day ahead to eat much.
She is too upset with Dad to eat much of the food he made.
She is too busy getting ready to eat much.

why.A: C is right. She reties both shoes and then checks one again, which is fussing over small things, so she is nervous about the concert. A is wrong: it is only seven o'clock, and the concert starts at ten. B: nothing in paragraph 1 is about Dad or a ride. D: she is already in her black concert shirt, and nothing says she might not play.
why.B: B is right. She takes one small bite of toast and unzips the pocket three times to check that her drumsticks are still there, so she is too nervous to eat. A: checking the pocket again and again does not fit being sleepy. C: Dad only offers her eggs; nothing shows she is upset with him. D: she is already sitting at the table.

questions.skill: Make an inference about a character (Part A)

prompt.A: Part A: Read paragraph 3. What can you infer about how Leo feels about his sister?
prompt.B: Part A: Read paragraphs 4-6. What is Marisol most likely feeling during the long quiet minute?

A: He looks up to her and wants to be like her.
He wants to show her that he can drum better than she can.
He wants her to stop practicing and play a game with him.
He wants to bug her so that she will hurry up and leave.
B: She feels worried that Dad is upset with her.
She feels worried that the concert will start soon.
She feels sorry that Abuela had to fly so far.
She feels sorry that she hurt Leo's feelings.

why.A: A is right. Leo plays the same beat Marisol practiced every night for a month and looks up at her with a huge grin, so he wants to be like her. B: when she says he is doing it wrong, he does not argue; his grin disappears. C: she is eating breakfast, not practicing, and he never asks to play a game. D: nothing in the story shows he wants her to leave.
why.B: D is right. She has just made Leo's grin disappear, and she ends the quiet by giving him her sticks and helping him. That shows she feels bad. A: Dad says nothing, and she turns to Leo, not Dad. B: she looks at the clock, but it is seven and the concert is at ten. C: the story never says Abuela's trip was hard or that Marisol feels sorry about it.

questions.skill: Choose evidence that supports an inference (Part B)

prompt.A: Part B: Which detail BEST supports your answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which detail from the story BEST supports your answer to Part A?

A: He looked up at her with a huge grin. (paragraph 3)
Across the table, her little brother Leo grabbed two spoons. (paragraph 3)
He set the spoons down slowly and stared at his cereal. (paragraph 4)
It was the same beat Marisol had practiced every night for a month. (paragraph 3)
B: Leo's grin disappeared. (paragraph 4)
Dad poured his coffee and said nothing. (paragraph 6)
"Hold them like this," she said quietly, moving his fingers. (paragraph 7)
Marisol looked at the clock. (paragraph 5)

why.A: D is right. Leo plays HER beat, the one she practiced every night for a month, so he is copying her. A shows he wants her to see him, but alone it could also back 'show her he can drum better' or 'bug her.' B shows only that he picked up spoons. C shows how he feels after she snaps, not why he played.
why.B: C is right. Right after the quiet minute she speaks quietly and helps Leo hold the sticks, which shows she is sorry for snapping. A shows that Leo was hurt, but not how Marisol feels about it. B is about Dad (it could seem to back 'Dad is upset'). D could seem to back 'worried about the time,' but looking at a clock shows nothing about how she feels toward Leo.

questions.skill: Judge which evidence best proves a claim

prompt.A: A classmate says, "Marisol cares about Leo, even when she is stressed." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?
prompt.B: A classmate says, "Thinking about Abuela makes Marisol fidget." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?

A: "Leo, stop it!" Marisol snapped. (paragraph 4)
Marisol did not say anything either for a long minute. (paragraph 6)
Under the table, Marisol's fingers drummed on her knee. (paragraph 5)
She slid them across the table to Leo. (paragraph 6)
B: Then she looked at the photo on the fridge of Abuela waving from an airport. ... Under the table, Marisol's fingers drummed on her knee. (paragraph 5)
Then she looked at the photo on the fridge of Abuela waving from an airport. ... today she would finally hear it in person. (paragraph 5)
She bent down and retied her left shoe. ... Then she checked the left one again. (paragraph 1)
Dad poured his coffee and said nothing. ... Then she reached into her backpack and pulled out her practice sticks, the old ones with the chipped tips. (paragraph 6)

why.A: D is right. 'Them' are her own practice sticks, and she gives them to Leo before she has calmed down: so far she has taken only one small bite of toast, and she eats the whole piece only at the end (paragraph 8). So she cares about him even while she is stressed. A shows the stress but not the caring. B is the quiet minute before she acts; being quiet alone does not show what she feels about Leo. C shows she is tense, but it shows nothing about Leo.
why.B: A is right. In the same paragraph, she looks at Abuela's photo, and a little later her fingers drum on her knee under the table. So it links her fidgeting to Abuela. B tells why Abuela matters, but it shows no fidgeting at all. C shows fidgeting, but it is in paragraph 1 and says nothing about Abuela. D shows what she does after the quiet minute; it is about Leo, and it shows no fidgeting and no link to Abuela.

questions.skill: Why the author included a detail (story)

prompt.A: Read paragraph 5. Why does the author include the photo of Abuela on the fridge?
prompt.B: Read paragraph 8. Why does the author end the story this way?

A: To hint that Marisol is sad because Abuela lives so far away.
To hint at why this concert matters so much to Marisol.
To hint that Marisol is waiting for Abuela to call her.
To hint that Abuela is the one who taught Marisol to drum.
B: To show that Marisol is still too nervous to talk to Leo.
To show that Marisol eats to please Dad before they leave.
To show that Marisol feels calmer than she did before.
To show that Marisol forgives Leo for copying her beat.

why.A: B is right. The photo leads to the news that Abuela landed last night and today will finally hear Marisol play in person, so this concert matters a lot. A and C are wrong because Abuela is already here; she landed last night. D: the story never says who taught Marisol to drum.
why.B: C is right. Earlier she took only one small bite of toast. Now, after she helps Leo, she eats the whole piece, so she is calmer. A: she has just talked to Leo and shown him how to hold the sticks. B: Dad offered her eggs at the start, but paragraph 8 says nothing about Dad or leaving, and the concert is hours away. D is backward: Leo did nothing wrong, and she was the one who snapped.

sections.heading: Passage 2: The Crow Next Door
sections.directions: [1] You have probably seen a crow picking through trash or calling from a power line. Many people think of crows as noisy pests. But scientists have found that the crows living in our cities may be some of the smartest animals around.

[2] Crows can remember human faces. In one set of studies, researchers wore a certain mask while they caught a few crows, checked them, and let them go unharmed. Later, whenever someone walked by wearing that mask, crows scolded loudly and dove toward it. This kept happening for years. Even more surprising, crows that had never been caught joined in the scolding. Some of them had not even hatched when the first crows were caught.

[3] Crows also solve problems with tools. Some crows poke sticks into holes to pull out bugs. In tests, crows have bent a piece of wire into a hook to lift a small basket of food out of a tube. New Caledonian crows, which live on islands in the Pacific Ocean, are especially skilled with tools.

[4] City crows have found their own tricks. Some have been seen dropping hard nuts onto busy roads. When a car rolls over a nut and cracks it, the crow waits for a break in traffic. Then it flies down to eat.

[5] When a crow dies, other crows often gather around it and call loudly. To a person watching, this can look like a funeral. Some scientists think the crows are studying the scene. They may be learning what to stay away from.
[6] So the next time a crow watches you from a fence, remember that it may be paying close attention. It might even remember you.

sections.heading: Questions 6-10
sections.directions: Use Passage 2, "The Crow Next Door," to answer questions 6-10.

prompt.A: Read paragraph 4 again. Think about when the crow flies down to eat. What does this suggest about the crow?
prompt.B: Read paragraph 2 again. What does it suggest about crows?

A: It understands that it must wait until a car has cracked the nut.
It understands that the cars on the road could hit it.
It understands that the nut is too hot to eat right away.
It understands that people in the cars might be watching it.
B: Crows can learn about a person from other crows.
Crows can learn to scold any person who walks by them.
Crows can learn to trust a person who let other crows go.
Crows can pick out a new face after seeing it just one time.

why.A: B is right. The crow waits for a break in traffic before it flies down, so it seems to know the cars could hurt it. A: the car has already cracked the nut when the crow waits; it is waiting for the traffic, not the nut. C: nothing says the nut is hot. D: the paragraph never mentions drivers watching the crow.
why.B: A is right. Crows that had never been caught joined in the scolding, and some had not even hatched when the first crows were caught, so they seem to have learned about the mask from other crows. B: they scolded people wearing that one mask, not everyone who walked by. C: the researchers let the caught crows go unharmed, but the crows scolded the mask instead of trusting it. D: the article says the scolding kept happening for years, but it never says how fast a crow learns a face.

questions.skill: Make an inference from an article (Part A)

prompt.A: Part A: What can you infer about the author's view of crows?
prompt.B: Part A: Read paragraph 2. What did the crows most likely believe about the person in the mask?

A: The author thinks crows are smart, but less smart than scientists once believed.
The author thinks city crows are smarter than crows that live in the wild.
The author thinks crows are smarter than many people give them credit for.
The author thinks crows are smart because they copy what people do.
B: That the person had once helped them.
That the person was someone they did not know.
That the person was afraid of them.
That the person was a danger to them.

why.A: C is right. The author says many people think of crows as noisy pests, then shows how smart they are. A: the article never says scientists once thought crows were smarter; it says scientists found they may be some of the smartest animals around. B: the article never compares city crows with wild crows, and it calls New Caledonian crows on Pacific islands especially skilled with tools. D: the article shows crows learning from other crows and solving problems, not copying people.
why.B: D is right. The crows scolded loudly and dove toward the mask, so they treated the person in it as a threat. A: the researchers did let the crows go unharmed, but the crows scolded the mask instead of acting friendly. B: the crows remembered the mask; the scolding kept happening for years. C: the crows were the ones scolding and diving; nothing shows the person was afraid of them.

questions.skill: Choose evidence that supports an inference (Part B)

prompt.A: Part B: Which detail BEST supports your answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which detail from the article BEST supports your answer to Part A?

A: Many people think of crows as noisy pests. (paragraph 1)
But scientists have found that the crows living in our cities may be some of the smartest animals around. (paragraph 1)
City crows have found their own tricks. (paragraph 4)
Crows also solve problems with tools. (paragraph 3)
B: In one set of studies, researchers wore a certain mask while they caught a few crows, checked them, and let them go unharmed. (paragraph 2)
Crows can remember human faces. (paragraph 2)
Later, whenever someone walked by wearing that mask, crows scolded loudly and dove toward it. (paragraph 2)
It might even remember you. (paragraph 6)

why.A: B is right. 'But' sets what scientists found against what many people think, so the author thinks crows get too little credit. A gives only what many people think, not the author's view. C could seem to back 'city crows are smarter,' but it does not compare them with any other crows. D shows crows are clever, but it does not set that against what people believe.
why.B: C is right. Scolding loudly and diving toward the mask shows the crows treated its wearer as a threat. A is the cause: it tells why the crows linked the mask to being caught, but not what they believed (and 'unharmed' could seem to back 'had once helped them'). B shows crows remember faces, but not what they think of this person. D is about the reader, not the person in the mask.

questions.skill: Judge which evidence best proves a claim

prompt.A: A student says, "Crows pass what they know on to other crows." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?
prompt.B: A student says, "City crows can plan a few steps ahead." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?

A: Even more surprising, crows that had never been caught joined in the scolding. (paragraph 2)
You have probably seen a crow picking through trash or calling from a power line. (paragraph 1)
When a crow dies, other crows often gather around it and call loudly. (paragraph 5)
Crows can remember human faces. (paragraph 2)
B: Some have been seen dropping hard nuts onto busy roads. (paragraph 4)
When a car rolls over a nut and cracks it, the crow waits for a break in traffic. (paragraph 4)
Then it flies down to eat. (paragraph 4)
New Caledonian crows, which live on islands in the Pacific Ocean, are especially skilled with tools. (paragraph 3)

why.A: A is right. These crows were never caught, yet they joined in scolding the mask, so they seem to have learned about it from other crows. B shows a crow calling, not one crow passing what it knows to another. C shows crows gathering and calling, but it does not show one crow passing what it knows to another. D shows that a crow can remember a face, not that it passes what it knows to another crow.
why.B: B is right. After a car cracks the nut, the crow waits for a break in traffic before it goes for the food, so it is doing one step, waiting, and then the next. A shows only the first step; alone it does not show what the crow does next. C shows only the last step. D says some crows are skilled with tools, but it does not show a crow planning steps.

questions.skill: Why the author included a detail (article)

prompt.A: Read paragraph 5. Why does the author say the scene can look like a funeral?
prompt.B: Read paragraph 6. Why does the author end the article this way?

A: To help readers picture the scene by comparing it to something they know.
To help readers see that crows feel sad the way people do.
To suggest that the crows gather to keep people and other animals away from the dead crow.
To suggest that the crows around the dead crow are all one family.
B: To suggest that readers should feed the crows near their homes.
To suggest that the crows near readers' homes may be dangerous to people.
To suggest that city crows are smarter than crows on islands.
To connect the article's ideas to things readers may see every day.

why.A: A is right. The author says the scene 'can look like' a funeral, comparing it to something readers know. B: the next sentences say some scientists think the crows are studying the scene, not that they feel sad. C and D are never said in the article.
why.B: D is right. The ending turns to a crow on the reader's own fence, linking the studies to everyday life. A: the article never tells readers to feed crows. B: the ending says a crow may pay attention and might remember you, not that it will hurt you. C: paragraph 3 says New Caledonian crows on Pacific islands are especially skilled with tools; the article never says city crows are smarter.

sections.heading: SHORT RESPONSE (4 points)
sections.directions: Use Passage 1, "Ba-da-bum." Write in complete sentences. Remember C-E-E: Claim, Evidence, Explanation. Check your answer with the rubric before you turn it in.

questions.skill: Constructed response: inference with two pieces of evidence (C-E-E)

prompt.A: Think about how Marisol acts before and after she snaps at Leo. What does this show about her as a person? Use TWO pieces of evidence from the story. Name the paragraph for each one, and explain how it supports your idea.
prompt.B: What can you infer about what kind of person Marisol is? Use TWO pieces of evidence from the story. Name the paragraph for each, and explain how each one proves your idea.

answer.A: Marisol gets tense under pressure, but she is caring and can fix her own mistakes. In paragraph 4 she snaps at Leo and calls his beat wrong, so the stress makes her sharp with him. In paragraphs 6–7 she notices how quiet he has gone, gives him her old practice sticks, and gently shows him how to hold them. That shows she cares about him and wants to make things right after hurting his feelings.
answer.B: Strong answer: Marisol is a caring sister, even when she is stressed. In paragraph 4 she snaps at Leo, but in paragraph 6 she slides her old practice sticks to him. This shows she feels bad and wants to make it right. In paragraph 7 she speaks quietly and tells him he can sit in the front row and watch her hands. This shows she wants him to feel included in her big day. (Other supported inferences are fine, e.g., she is nervous because Abuela will hear her play for the first time, as long as two details really support the claim and are explained.)

why.A: Score with the C-E-E rubric. Look for an inference the story never states outright, two details that each support it, and an explanation of how each detail shows the inference.
why.B: Score with the C-E-E rubric. A retelling of what happens ("She gave Leo the sticks") is a detail, not an inference; the claim must go beyond what the text says.

documents.title: SHORT RESPONSE SELF-CHECK: C-E-E
documents.directions: Before you turn in your short response, read each row. Circle the box that matches your answer. If two boxes fit, circle the lower one. For each piece of evidence, ask yourself: If this were the ONLY sentence I had, would it prove my answer? If any row is below 4, fix that part of your answer first!

rubric.title: What can you infer about the character? (4 points)

criteria.name: Claim (my inference)
levels: I wrote a clear inference about the character. The story does not say it outright. I figured it out from clues.
I wrote an inference, but it is a little unclear or very general (like "She is nice").
My claim just repeats something the story says in plain words (like "Marisol plays the drums").
I did not write a claim, or I guessed with no clues.

criteria.name: Evidence (proof from the text)
levels: I used TWO pieces of evidence. I named the paragraph for each one. Each one really proves my inference.
I used two pieces of evidence, but only one really proves my inference. Or I forgot to name a paragraph.
I used two pieces, but neither one really proves my inference. Or I used only one piece of evidence.
I did not use evidence from the story.

criteria.name: Explanation (how it proves it)
levels: For each piece of evidence, I explained HOW it shows my inference ("This shows that...").
I explained one piece of evidence well. For the other one, I did not explain it or I only repeated it.
I tried to explain, but I mostly repeated the evidence.
I did not explain how my evidence connects to my inference.

rubric.note: This task is worth 4 points in all, not 4 points for each row. Here is how to find your score: 1. Circle the level (4, 3, 2 or 1) that fits each row. 2. Add your three numbers. 3. Use your total: 11 or 12 = 4 points. 8, 9 or 10 = 3 points. 5, 6 or 7 = 2 points. 3 or 4 = 1 point.

facts.notes: The crow article holds up against the teacher's notes and published research (the Marzluff/Cornell mask studies, Weir et al. 2002 wire hook, the Sendai nut-dropping crows, Swift & Marzluff 2015 on dead crows). The problems are in the question wording: one evidence choice misstates paragraph 4, one adds a detail to paragraph 3, and one why line claims more than the passage says. Two simplifications go to the teacher. No web search was run; references are from known published studies.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9 choice A (key)
findings.what: The choice says the crow 'sets' a nut on the road and 'waits for a car to crack it'. Paragraph 4 says crows drop the nuts, and the waiting it describes comes after the car cracks the nut, when the crow waits for a break in traffic. Reword to match the passage, keeping the same answer.
findings.source: Passage 2 para 4
findings.before: A crow sets a nut on the road and waits for a car to crack it. (paragraph 4)
findings.fixed: Reworded to "A crow drops a nut on a busy road, then waits for a break in traffic to eat it." Same answer, now matches paragraph 4.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q6 why
findings.what: The explanation says the never-caught crows 'must have learned it from crows that were caught.' The passage only supports learning from other crows (some had not hatched yet, so they may have learned secondhand). Change to 'from other crows.'
findings.source: Passage 2 para 2; Cornell, Marzluff & Pecoraro 2012, Proc. R. Soc. B
findings.fixed: Now says "They must have learned it from other crows."

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q8 choice B
findings.what: The choice says New Caledonian crows live on islands 'far out in' the Pacific; the passage says only 'on islands in the Pacific Ocean,' and the why line calls this detail true. Drop 'far out'.
findings.source: Passage 2 para 3
findings.before: New Caledonian crows live on islands far out in the Pacific Ocean. (paragraph 3)
findings.fixed: The New Caledonian choice was replaced (round 2) with "Some city crows drop hard nuts onto busy roads."

findings.where: Passage 2 para 3 (wire hook sentence)
findings.what: 'In tests, crows have bent a piece of wire into a hook' describes work done mainly with one captive New Caledonian crow (Betty). Because the sentence comes before New Caledonian crows are named, students may think ordinary city crows do this. True as a simplification; the teacher may prefer 'In tests, a New Caledonian crow bent a piece of wire…'
findings.source: Weir, Chappell & Kacelnik 2002, Science

findings.where: Passage 2 para 4 / INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9 key and why
findings.what: Nut-dropping on roads is well documented (Sendai, Japan), but whether crows use cars on purpose is still debated (a Davis, California study found American crows did not drop more nuts when cars were coming). Inside the passage, the B q9 'plan with several steps' inference is defensible; the teacher may want to keep it as a passage-based inference only.
findings.source: Nihei 1995; Cristol, Switzer, Johnson & Walke 1997, Animal Behaviour

facts.notes: Checked every > line in changed-text.diff (q1-q10 versions A and B: prompts, all 80 choices, keys, why lines; the new rubric) against passages.md and the teacher's notes, plus the 9 science claims the crow article makes. Tally: 103 source, 14 reference, 5 off (FIX), 9 judgment. All 32 Part B / evidence choices are in the paragraph they cite (32/32 citations right). Every quoted choice matches the story or article word for word, or nearly so. Exceptions are noted as findings: q4 A choice B and q4 B choice C are each two sentences joined into one, and q9 B choice D is a paraphrase. Every key is defensible from the text. Rubric arithmetic checks out (row totals 3-12 map onto 1-4 with no gaps or overlaps; all 4s = 12 = 4 points, matching the teacher's '4 = all three strong'). Science: the article's claims are true or carefully hedged. Face and mask memory with social spread: Marzluff et al. 2010; Cornell, Marzluff & Pecoraro 2012. Wire hook: Weir, Chappell & Kacelnik 2002, where one New Caledonian crow named Betty bent the wire; rooks have also done it (Bird & Emery 2009), so the plural 'crows' holds. Sticks for grubs: Hunt 1996. New Caledonia is a group of islands in the southwest Pacific. Gathering around dead crows to learn about danger: Swift & Marzluff 2015. Nut dropping on roads: seen in Sendai (Nihei 1995; Nihei & Higuchi 2001), but a California study (Cristol et al. 1997) found car use there was coincidental. 'Have been seen' is accurate, but saying the crows plan it is a judgment. Out of scope (unchanged text), for whoever owns q11: key A says Marisol 'notices how quiet he has gone'. The story never says what she notices, so that wording is itself an inference. Time: about 25 minutes; tokens: about 70k.

Direction: give a true reason, e.g. 'C: Dad offers eggs at the start, but he says nothing at the end, and nothing shows she eats to please him; she eats after helping Leo.'

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q6 (why, reason for A)

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q6 (key and why)
findings.what: The key and the why line say the crow 'knows' cars are dangerous. The article says only that it waits for a break in traffic, and 'knows' is the inference the question asks for. Studies of birds near roads support the idea that they treat traffic as danger, but what a crow understands is not directly shown. This is acceptable for an inference key. If the teacher wants to model hedged language, use 'It seems to understand that moving cars can hurt it.'
findings.source: passages.md Passage 2 ¶4; Legagneux & Ducatez 2013, 'European birds adjust their flight initiation distance to road speed limits', Biology Letters 9:20130417

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q9 (why, key)
findings.what: 'they could only know about the mask from other crows' is strong for choice C taken alone. Without the next sentence ('some had not even hatched'), a crow that was never caught might have watched the capture. The real study does count both kinds as social learning, so the key is right, but 'could only' overclaims for C alone. Direction (optional): 'so they most likely learned about the mask from other crows.' The q6 B key ('Crows can learn about danger from other crows') is KEEP: the study supports it directly.
findings.source: passages.md Passage 2 ¶2; Cornell, Marzluff & Pecoraro 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234554/

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9 (key choice D and why)
findings.what: There are two issues. (1) The why says the crow 'lets a car crack it', but choice D as written leaves out the car ('dropped a hard nut onto a busy road, then waited for a break in traffic'). The why describes the article, not the choice. (2) 'That is a plan with several steps' is stated as fact. The science on deliberate car use is mixed: Sendai crows look deliberate, while California crows' car use was found to be coincidental. Direction: restore the car step in choice D ('...a car cracked it, and the crow waited for a break in traffic to eat'), and write 'That looks like a plan with several steps.' Also, choice D is the only paraphrase among verbatim distractors (see the q4 finding).
findings.source: passages.md Passage 2 ¶4; Nihei 1995 / Nihei & Higuchi 2001 (Sendai carrion crows), https://tohoku.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/1503/files/0040-8743-2001-60-93.pdf; Cristol, Switzer, Johnson & Walke 1997, 'Crows do not use automobiles as nutcrackers', The Auk 114:296-298, https://sora-dev.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v114n02/p0296-p0298.pdf

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q4 (key choice C and why); also A q4 key choice B
findings.what: B q4 choice C ('She looked at the photo of Abuela, and under the table her fingers drummed on her knee') joins the first and last sentences of paragraph 5, which are separated by two others ('Abuela had landed last night. For two years...'). The why's 'right then' makes them sound back to back. It is the right paragraph and close wording, so it passes item 1. Two cautions: it reads as a quote but is not one, and the joining is what makes it the only choice that links Abuela and nerves. A q4 choice B likewise joins two sentences of paragraph 6. With B q9 D, these three keys are the only non-verbatim choices in sets where the distractors are exact sentences, a pattern a test-wise student could spot. Direction: hand to the assessment check. Either quote the keys as exact sentences (with an ellipsis where text is cut) or paraphrase the distractors too. Change 'right then' to 'in the same paragraph'.

findings.what: 'it says New Caledonian crows on Pacific islands are especially skilled' drops 'with tools'. The article says they are especially skilled with tools, not smarter overall. The clean reason is that the article never compares city crows with wild crows. Direction: 'B: the article never compares city crows with wild ones; the crows it calls especially skilled with tools live on Pacific islands.' (New Caledonia is a group of islands in the southwest Pacific: true.)

findings.source: passages.md Passage 2 ¶2; Marzluff et al. 2010, 'Lasting recognition of threatening people by wild American crows', Animal Behaviour 79:699-707

findings.what: The new level 4 requires 'I named the paragraph for each one', and level 3 adds 'Or I forgot to name a paragraph'. The teacher's notes allow either: 'Quote it or name the paragraph'. Under this rubric, a student who quotes exactly but names no paragraph drops a level. The q11 prompts do ask students to name the paragraph, so the rubric matches the prompt but not the notes. Teacher's call: either restore 'named the paragraph or quoted' or keep it as is.

findings.where: Passage 2 ¶4 and INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q6 (why)
findings.what: Nut dropping on roads: 'Some have been seen dropping hard nuts onto busy roads' is accurate (Sendai carrion crows). 'Waits for a break in traffic' matches the Sendai reports of crows collecting nuts at red lights. The why line's 'C: the car has already cracked the nut' matches the article.
findings.source: Nihei & Higuchi 2001, https://tohoku.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/1503/files/0040-8743-2001-60-93.pdf; caveat Cristol et al. 1997, The Auk 114:296-298

findings.where: Passage 2 ¶2 and INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q6 / B q6 / B q7 / B q8 (keys and whys)
findings.what: Mask studies: researchers wore a distinctive mask while trapping, banding and releasing crows near Seattle. Crows scolded and mobbed the mask for years, birds never trapped joined in, and young crows learned it from their parents. A neutral control mask was not scolded, which supports 'one certain mask, not every mask'. Mobbing is an anti-predator response, which supports 'a danger to them'.
findings.source: Marzluff et al. 2010, Animal Behaviour 79:699-707; Cornell, Marzluff & Pecoraro 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234554/

findings.where: Passage 2 ¶3 and INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q8 choice A, B q9 choice B
findings.what: Wire hook to lift a small basket (a bucket) of food from a tube: true. The original subject was one New Caledonian crow, Betty, and rooks have since done the same, so the plural 'crows have bent' is fair. New Caledonian crows poke sticks into holes for grubs (Hunt 1996, Nature). Calling stick use 'a one-step use of a tool' (B q9 why) fits the sentence as written, though in the wild New Caledonian crows also make their tools.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q6 (choice D + why)
findings.what: Choice D ('Crows can pick out a new face after seeing it just one time') can be defended from paragraph 2. The crows saw the mask while they were being caught, and later they scolded it for years, so a student can reasonably infer that one catching was enough. That is also close to what happened in the real study: crows trapped once while the researcher wore the mask scolded it for years. The why line ('it never says how fast a crow learns a face') does not make D false. Suggested direction: swap D for a choice paragraph 2 clearly rules out. Example: 'Crows forget a face after a few weeks'. This is wrong because the scolding 'kept happening for years' (paragraph 2). Rewrite the D part of the why line to match.
findings.source: passages.md P2 ¶2; Marzluff et al. 2010, 'Lasting recognition of threatening people by wild American crows,' Animal Behaviour 79:699-707, doi:10.1016/j.anbehav.2009.12.022 (crows trapped while the researcher wore a 'dangerous' mask; recognition lasted at least 2.7 years); BirdNote summary https://birdnote.org/node/11006

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q5 (why, reason for A)
findings.what: The why line says 'A and C are wrong because Abuela is already here; she landed last night.' That works for C (waiting for her to call) but not for A ('sad because Abuela lives so far away'). The story suggests Abuela really does live far away: two years of hearing about the drumming 'on the phone,' a photo 'waving from an airport,' and she 'landed.' Her being here now does not show Marisol isn't sad about the distance. Suggested direction: give A its own reason, e.g. 'A: nothing in paragraph 5 shows Marisol is sad; the photo leads straight to the news that Abuela will hear her play in person today (paragraph 5).' Keep 'she landed last night' as the reason for C only.
findings.source: passages.md P1 ¶5

sameAs.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q5

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q2 (why, reason for C)
findings.what: The why line says 'she is eating breakfast, not practicing.' In paragraph 2 she pushes her eggs around and takes one small bite of toast. She is hardly eating, and B q1 and B q5 both depend on that. Suggested direction: 'C: she is sitting at breakfast, not practicing (paragraph 2), and Leo never asks to play a game.'
findings.source: passages.md P1 ¶2, ¶3

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q1 (why, reason for D)
findings.what: 'D: she is already sitting at the table' is true (paragraph 1), but it doesn't rule out 'too busy getting ready.' A student could point to her checking the backpack as getting ready. The reason students can learn: she isn't doing new jobs. She checks the same pocket three times, which is fussing, not being busy. Suggested direction: 'D: she is not doing a list of jobs; she unzips the same pocket three times to check the same drumsticks (paragraph 2), which shows worry, not being busy.'
findings.source: passages.md P1 ¶2

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9 (key B, why) and A q6
findings.what: Whether crows use cars on purpose as nutcrackers is debated. Nihei (1995) recorded carrion crows in Sendai, Japan, putting walnuts where cars would crack them. Cristol et al. (1997) found American crows in Davis, California, were no more likely to drop walnuts when a car was coming. The article hedges ('have been seen'), and A q6's why says 'seems to know,' which is fine. B q9's claim that crows 'plan a few steps ahead' rests on this contested behavior. Also, on the article's own terms, choice A ('dropping hard nuts onto busy roads') arguably shows planning ahead too, because a crow that picks a BUSY road expects cars. The key B (car cracks the nut, crow waits for traffic) shows two steps and is still the best answer. The teacher may want to accept a well-argued A in discussion, or change the why for A to: 'A shows where the crow drops the nut, but alone it does not show the crow waiting for the right moment.'
findings.source: passages.md P2 ¶4; Nihei 1995, carrion crows using automobiles to crack walnuts, Sendai (Tohoku Univ. record https://tohoku.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/1503/files/0040-8743-2001-60-93.pdf); Cristol, Switzer, Johnson & Walke 1997, 'Crows do not use automobiles as nutcrackers: putting an anecdote to the test,' The Auk 114:296-298 https://sora-dev.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v114n02/p0296-p0298.pdf

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q4 (key D)
findings.what: The stem asks which detail, 'if it were the ONLY one you had,' would best prove 'Marisol cares about Leo, even when she is stressed.' The key, 'She slid them across the table to Leo,' read on its own, doesn't say what 'them' is or show any stress. The why line has to pull in paragraphs 6 and 8 to make the case. Everything the why line says is true, and D is still the best of the four. But the 'ONLY sentence' test the teacher teaches doesn't really work for this key. Option: quote the whole sentence pair from paragraph 6 ('Then she reached into her backpack and pulled out her practice sticks, the old ones with the chipped tips. She slid them across the table to Leo.'), or accept it as is.
findings.source: passages.md P1 ¶6, ¶8; sources/inference-lesson-notes.md ('If this sentence were the only one I had...')

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q4 (stem, key A, why)
findings.what: The key treats 'fingers drummed on her knee' as fidgeting. The teacher's notes support that reading ('she is nervous (actions: retying shoes, tapping...)'). But Marisol is a drummer, so some students will read it as running through her part. The link to Abuela also comes from order in the paragraph (photo, then Abuela's news, then drumming), not from anything that says it's the cause. The why line keeps its wording modest ('links'), and A is still clearly the best choice. No change is needed if the teacher is happy with 'fidget.'
findings.source: passages.md P1 ¶5; sources/inference-lesson-notes.md

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q6, A q9, B q7 (crows learn about the mask from other crows; scolding for years; unhatched crows)
findings.what: Reference: confirmed. Crows that were never caught learned to scold the 'dangerous' mask (horizontal social learning), and young crows learned it from their parents (vertical social learning), which matches 'had not even hatched.' The why lines say 'seem to have learned,' which is the right strength.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q10 (why) / Passage 2 ¶5
findings.what: Reference: confirmed. Crows gather and mob around a dead crow and afterward avoid the people and places linked with it. 'Some scientists think... they may be learning what to stay away from' is accurate and suitably hedged. The why for B ('not that they feel sad') is true to the article.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q8 D, B q10 C, A q7 B (tools, wire hook, New Caledonian crows)

Wild New Caledonian crows use sticks to pull larvae out of holes. New Caledonia is a group of islands in the southwest Pacific. Note: the wire-hook test used a New Caledonian crow, not a city crow, and the article doesn't claim otherwise. A 2021 re-analysis (van Buuren et al.) questions how new Betty's bending was, but not that it happened.

findings.where: SHORT RESPONSE SELF-CHECK: C-E-E (rubric)
findings.what: Read as a student: (1) 'If you are not at a 4 yet, fix your answer first!' is ambiguous. A 4 in every row, or 4 points overall? Direction: add 'If two boxes fit, circle the lower one.' (3) Claim levels 2 ('repeats something the story says') and 1 ('only retold what happened') are hard for a 7th grader to tell apart. Direction: make level 1 'I did not write a claim, or I guessed with no clues.' (4) The 'ONLY sentence' reminder is tacked onto the end of the scoring steps; move it to the Evidence row or the directions.

Ms. Okafor (made-up sample) ordered a grade 7 ELA quiz with A/B versions on making inferences and citing text evidence, plus a rubric for its short response. The maker wrote two original passages from her lesson notes, a story and an article, and 22 question rows. Five rounds of checks followed (rounds 4 and 5 were extra rounds the owner, acting as the teacher, chose after round 3), each by agents that had not written the work; every round caught something the round before had missed or created.

Round 1 (14:15–14:40). The maker needed four drafts to get past the lead's pre-checks: on the first draft one test-wise bot (oddOne) picked the key 55% of the time against 25% chance. The fact checker checked 47 claims and flagged 5: 3 to fix and 2 for the teacher. The blind tester first answered all 20 multiple-choice items WITHOUT the passages and matched 20 of 20 keys, 17 at high confidence: a student who skipped the reading could have aced it. Wilco's bots had passed the same quiz at 30%, because the cue was in the content (only the key sounded like a teacher's answer), which the bots can't see. The blind tester listed 11 FIX.

Round 2 (14:44–14:57). A new maker session got only the FIX list and rewrote wrong choices on 18 items, using real details from the passages. Wilco failed it at once: the new wrong choices all borrowed the key's idea, so the 'converge' bot found the key 50% of the time. After a rewording it passed at 31%. A different fresh blind tester confirmed 7 fixes in full and 3 in part, and caught 2 new problems the fixes had created: A q4 and B q9 now had two right answers.

Round 3 (15:00–15:16). A third maker session fixed both two-right items, rewrote one wrong choice on 10 items so a reader who skipped the passage has a believable trap, and rewrote the rubric's scoring note after the lead saw '4 pts' print on every row of a test render (reading as 12 points). Wilco failed twice more (a trained bot at 50% on version B, then the 'middle length' bot at 38%) and passed on the third try at 31%. A third fresh blind tester confirmed the fixes and was the first checker to read the rubric.

Round 4 (extra, 16:13–16:31). A fresh maker session (9.2 minutes) got the FIX list only: the passage-free problem plus the 5 open round 3 items. It rewrote every question stem and most wrong choices, and ran the key and test-wise checks itself (rounds 1–3 needed 8 lead relays). Wilco passed: worst middleValue 31%, converge 30%, longest 28%, chance 25%. The fresh blind recheck confirmed all 5 open round 3 items fixed, but still matched 20 of 20 without the passages (18 at confidence 4–5, up from 15) and found 8 new FIX: the passage-free problem again, B q8 (the key said the cause but did not prove what the crows believed), A q4 and B q9 (the key was the only choice that fit, or the only stitched quote), B q4, B q7, the 'why did the author' items A q5, A q10 and B q10 (the mild choice was always the key), and the rubric (four unclear scoring steps). It also gave 4 JUDGMENT and 4 KEEP. The fact checker checked 131 claims and flagged 14: 5 FIX (five why lines that said more than the text does) and 9 JUDGMENT; 32 of 32 evidence choices sit in the paragraph they cite. Wilco before and after: round 3 worst 31% (middleValue) → round 4 worst 31% (middleValue), all under the 35% line.

Round 5 (extra, 16:32–16:49). A second fresh maker session (9.5 minutes) got only the new FIX list. It made the B q8 key the exact paragraph 2 scolding-and-diving sentence (a key change), made the B q9 key the exact paragraph 4 sentence, reworded the rubric, and corrected the five why lines the fact checker flagged. The blind recheck confirmed the B q8, B q9 and rubric fixes, and the fact checker confirmed the five why-line fixes with no wrong key. The blind tester still matched 20 of 20 without the passages (16 confident) and found 15 FIX entries: 9 new and 6 repeats of round 4 findings (passage-free, A q4, B q4, B q7, B q10, levels). The new ones are A q6 (two right answers), A q11, A q9, A q7, A q8, B q3, A q5 (why line), and two rubric items (no 0 rule; boxes 3 and 2 overlap). It also gave 2 JUDGMENT and 3 KEEP. The fact checker checked 203 claims and flagged 8: 4 FIX (B q6 choice D, A q5 which matches the blind finding, A q2 and B q1 why lines) and 4 JUDGMENT. Wilco before and after: round 4 worst middleValue 31% → round 5 worst middle 31%, notLongest 28%, notVote 28%, chance 25%, all passes.

Passage-free probes (multiple choice only, 10 per version, chance 25%, the owner's fail line about 40%): version A before round 4 10 of 10 (10 at confidence 4–5) → after round 4 10 of 10 (6) → after round 5 9 of 10 (7). Version B before round 4 10 of 10 (9) → after round 4 10 of 10 (7) → after round 5 9 of 10 (6). The round's own blind tester, who sees both versions together, went 20 of 20 in every round: 17, 17, 15 confident in rounds 1–3, then 18 (round 4) and 16 (round 5). The goal was not met: a student who skips the reading would still get about 90% in either version, far above the 40% line. The two extra rounds changed which cues are left (fewer stems naming the answer, more Part A/Part B and author's-purpose cues) but did not remove them. With the passages the tester matched 20 of 20 in both rounds.

Catches in all (five rounds): 103 findings, 7 of them the same problem found again in a later round and counted once. 47 needed a fix: 30 were fixed and 17 are open after round 5 (listed first above). 27 were looked at and kept on purpose, and 29 are judgment calls left for the teacher. All 5 items left open after round 3 were confirmed fixed in round 4. Of the 13 round 4 FIX, 8 were confirmed fixed in round 5 (the 5 fact-checker why lines, B q8, B q9 and the rubric); the passage-free problem, A q4, B q4, B q7 and the author's-purpose keys stayed open. Round 5 also found new problems its own fixes made or exposed (A q6 two right answers, A q4 giving away A q11, B q3's paragraph range), as rounds 2 and 3 did.
